title: Inferring the age and sex of ancient potters from fingerprint ridge densities
author: Burchill, Sanders, et al.

steps.title: Prepare fingerprint dataset
steps.instruction: Include only fingerprint impressions that have at least six ridges averaged; preferably retain only those with ten or more ridges averaged to reduce noise.

steps.title: Examine MRB distribution and CV
steps.instruction: Plot the distribution of mean ridge breadth (MRB) values and compute the coefficient of variation (CV) of the dataset; use the CV to roughly classify the assemblage as Type 1 (low variation, likely single‑sex adults), Type 2 (moderate variation, mixed adults), or Type 3 (high variation, adults + children). This classification guides whether the Bayesian model will be run in a single‑sex or two‑sex version.

steps.title: Filter reference sample
steps.instruction: According to the assemblage type determined above, filter the modern reference data (Králík & Novotný): for Type 1 keep only males aged ≥ 15 years; for Type 2 keep males and females aged ≥ 15 years; for Type 3 keep the entire reference sample.

steps.title: Determine scaling factor
steps.instruction: Calculate the 95th percentile of MRB values in the archaeological dataset and the 95th percentile of MRB in the filtered reference dataset; compute the scaling factor as the ratio of the reference percentile to the archaeological percentile. Optionally repeat using the 97.5th percentile (results are similar).

steps.title: Apply scaling factor
steps.instruction: Multiply every MRB value in the archaeological dataset by the scaling factor obtained in the previous step so that the two distributions become comparable.

steps.title: Create homogeneous sub‑sets
steps.instruction: If the site contains distinct ceramic types or periods, split the scaled MRB data into self‑consistent categories (e.g., full‑sized pottery, miniatures, figurines) and treat each subset separately in subsequent analyses.

steps.title: Set up Bayesian mixture model
steps.instruction: In R, load the ‘rjags’ package and specify a Bayesian mixture model with the following priors: a flat (uniform) prior for the sex proportion (0–1); weakly informative priors for male and female age means (most likely ≈ 20 years, plausible 5–45 years) and age standard deviations (plausible up to 35 years); large‑variance priors for the asymptotic MRB growth parameters (Asym, R0, lrc) taken from the Králík & Novotný regression; and a normal likelihood for observed MRB with standard deviation σ. Define separate gamma age distributions for each sex.

steps.title: Run MCMC sampling
steps.instruction: Execute the model with 10 parallel Markov chains; continue sampling until the effective sample size for every parameter exceeds 3000 and the upper bound of the Gelman‑Rubin convergence diagnostic is ≤ 1.01.

steps.title: Extract posterior estimates
steps.instruction: From the converged chains obtain posterior distributions for: (a) the population‑level sex proportion, (b) the gamma‑distributed age parameters for males and females, and (c) the individual‑level age and sex of each fingerprint. Summarize results as probability distributions rather than single point estimates.

steps.title: Model comparison (optional)
steps.instruction: Fit alternative models such as (i) “two sexes, one shared age distribution”, (ii) “one sex, two age distributions”, and (iii) simpler mixture models; combine them in a super‑model and compute Bayes factors to identify the most parsimonious model that still explains the data.

steps.title: Validate with simulated data
steps.instruction: Generate 540 simulated datasets varying sample size (50, 100, 200), female proportion (10 %, 30 %, 50 %, 70 %, 90 %), mean ages (15, 20, 30 years) and age‑SDs (2 or 8 years) for each sex. Convert simulated MRB to ridge density (RD) as the inverse (MRB ≈ 1/RD). Round RD up to the nearest integer for women and down for men. Use a logistic‑regression‑derived RD threshold of 14.9 ridges/25 mm² (instead of the classic 13) for the KAmod2 model. Apply all models (Bayesian, KAmod2, random, etc.) to each simulated set, compute inferred total mean age, % females, mean ages per sex, and age‑class percentages, then compare these estimates to the known simulated values.
